questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Aluminium sulfate, ammonium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide contain compound ions. (a) State the formula and charge of sulfate, ammonium, carbonate and hydroxide ions. (b) Deduce the chemical formula of each compound using electrical neutrality. (c) Describe ionic bonding in a solid crystal rather than as a single isolated pair of ions.
markPoints: Sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻.
Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻.
Hydroxide is OH⁻.
Aluminium sulfate is Al₂(SO₄)₃ since 2×3+ balances 3×2−.
Ammonium carbonate is (NH₄)₂CO₃ since 2 NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻.
Magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)₂ since Mg²⁺ requires two OH⁻.
Ionic bonding is strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions arranged in a giant 3D lattice.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻. Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Hydroxide is OH⁻. Aluminium sulfate is Al₂(SO₄)₃ since 2×3+ balances 3×2−. Ammonium carbonate is (NH₄)₂CO₃ since 2 NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻. Magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)₂ since Mg²⁺ requires two OH⁻. Ionic bonding is strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions arranged in a giant 3D lattice.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Ammonia can react with a hydrogen ion to form NH₄⁺; ammonia can also form a compound with BF₃. (a) Explain how a dative covalent bond forms. (b) Identify the electron-pair donor and acceptor in each case. (c) Explain how a coordinate covalent bond is represented and whether the N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ remain distinguishable once formed.
markPoints: A coordinate covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons in which both electrons originate from one atom.
Ammonia's nitrogen has a lone electron pair that can be donated.
In NH₃ + H⁺, N is the donor and H⁺ the acceptor.
In NH₃→BF₃, N is the donor and electron-deficient boron is the acceptor.
Draw the coordinate arrow from N/lone-pair donor to the acceptor.
In the ammonium ion the four N–H bonds are equivalent; coordinate describes electron-pair origin, not a distinct lasting bond type.

In NH₃ + H⁺, N is the donor and H⁺ the acceptor. In NH₃→BF₃, N is the donor and electron-deficient boron is the acceptor. Draw the coordinate arrow from N/lone-pair donor to the acceptor. In the ammonium ion the four N–H bonds are equivalent; coordinate describes electron-pair origin, not a distinct lasting bond type.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Solid magnesium conducts electricity and can be bent without cracking, whereas solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity and is brittle. Explain both properties of each solid using precise models of metallic and ionic bonding.
markPoints: Magnesium has positive metal ions in a lattice attracted to delocalised mobile electrons.
The electrons can move through solid magnesium and carry charge, making it a conductor.
Layers of positive ions can shift while the delocalised electrons maintain metallic attraction, so it is malleable.
Sodium chloride has a giant lattice of alternating oppositely charged ions.
Ions are fixed in the solid lattice, so no mobile charged particles conduct electricity.
When an ionic lattice shifts, ions of like charge may become adjacent and strongly repel.
This repulsion can fracture an ionic crystal, explaining its brittleness.
Molten or dissolved NaCl can conduct because its ions can move.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium has positive metal ions in a lattice attracted to delocalised mobile electrons. The electrons can move through solid magnesium and carry charge, making it a conductor. Layers of positive ions can shift while the delocalised electrons maintain metallic attraction, so it is malleable. Sodium chloride has a giant lattice of alternating oppositely charged ions. Ions are fixed in the solid lattice, so no mobile charged particles conduct electricity. When an ionic lattice shifts, ions of like charge may become adjacent and strongly repel. This repulsion can fracture an ionic crystal, explaining its brittleness. Molten or dissolved NaCl can conduct because its ions can move.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A student is given crystalline diamond, graphite, solid iodine, solid sodium chloride and solid magnesium. (a) Classify each into one of the four AQA crystal structure types. (b) Explain their differences in electrical conductivity and melting behaviour. Include diamond and graphite in your explanation.
markPoints: Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent (macromolecular) carbon structures.
Iodine consists of simple molecular I₂ crystals held together by intermolecular London forces.
Solid NaCl forms a giant ionic lattice; magnesium forms a metallic lattice.
Diamond has four strong covalent bonds around each carbon and no mobile charges, so it is non-conducting and extremely high melting.
Graphite has three covalent bonds per carbon within layers, plus mobile delocalised electrons that conduct.
Graphite layers are held by weak attractions, but strong covalent bonding within layers explains its high melting temperature.
I₂ requires only intermolecular London attractions to be overcome for melting or sublimation, not breaking I–I covalent bonds.
Solid NaCl cannot conduct because ions are fixed; Mg conducts through mobile delocalised electrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent (macromolecular) carbon structures. Iodine consists of simple molecular I₂ crystals held together by intermolecular London forces. Solid NaCl forms a giant ionic lattice; magnesium forms a metallic lattice. Diamond has four strong covalent bonds around each carbon and no mobile charges, so it is non-conducting and extremely high melting. Graphite has three covalent bonds per carbon within layers, plus mobile delocalised electrons that conduct. Graphite layers are held by weak attractions, but strong covalent bonding within layers explains its high melting temperature. I₂ requires only intermolecular London attractions to be overcome for melting or sublimation, not breaking I–I covalent bonds. Solid NaCl cannot conduct because ions are fixed; Mg conducts through mobile delocalised electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain why solid ice is less dense than liquid water, why ice has a relatively high melting temperature for a small simple molecular substance, and which bonding interactions are disrupted on melting. Contrast this with the interactions overcome when solid iodine sublimes.
markPoints: Ice has a regular open, approximately tetrahedral network due to hydrogen bonds.
The open lattice leaves more space between water molecules than their average packing in liquid water.
Therefore ice has lower density and floats on liquid water.
Hydrogen bonding between H₂O molecules is stronger than the London forces expected from their molecular size alone.
Heating ice breaks/disrupts some intermolecular hydrogen bonds rather than covalent O–H bonds.
Iodine is molecular I₂; sublimation separates intact I₂ molecules by overcoming intermolecular London forces.
The covalent I–I bond remains intact on sublimation.
questions.modelAnswer: Ice has a regular open, approximately tetrahedral network due to hydrogen bonds. The open lattice leaves more space between water molecules than their average packing in liquid water. Therefore ice has lower density and floats on liquid water. Hydrogen bonding between H₂O molecules is stronger than the London forces expected from their molecular size alone. Heating ice breaks/disrupts some intermolecular hydrogen bonds rather than covalent O–H bonds. Iodine is molecular I₂; sublimation separates intact I₂ molecules by overcoming intermolecular London forces. The covalent I–I bond remains intact on sublimation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Use electron-pair repulsion to determine the shapes and approximate bond angles of BF₃, CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and NH₄⁺. Explain fully why water and ammonia have smaller bond angles than methane.
markPoints: BF₃ has three bonding regions and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, approximately 120°.
CH₄ has four bonding regions and no lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
NH₃ has three bonding regions and one lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.
H₂O has two bonding regions and two lone pairs: bent, about 104.5°.
NH₄⁺ has four bonding regions and no lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
Electron regions repel and arrange themselves to minimise repulsion.
Lone–lone repulsion > lone–bond repulsion > bond–bond repulsion.
One lone pair in NH₃ and two in H₂O compress their bond angles below methane's 109.5°.
questions.modelAnswer: BF₃ has three bonding regions and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, approximately 120°. CH₄ has four bonding regions and no lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5°. NH₃ has three bonding regions and one lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°. H₂O has two bonding regions and two lone pairs: bent, about 104.5°. NH₄⁺ has four bonding regions and no lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5°. Electron regions repel and arrange themselves to minimise repulsion. Lone–lone repulsion > lone–bond repulsion > bond–bond repulsion. One lone pair in NH₃ and two in H₂O compress their bond angles below methane's 109.5°.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A student compares CO₂, PCl₅, SF₆, SF₄ and XeF₄. (a) Give shape and characteristic bond angles of CO₂, PCl₅ and SF₆. (b) Explain the shapes of SF₄ and XeF₄ using bonding and lone pairs. (c) Explain why a double bond counts as a single region in VSEPR.
markPoints: CO₂ has two regions about carbon, so it is linear with 180° angle.
PCl₅ has five bonding regions and no lone pairs: trigonal bipyramidal with 90°, 120° and 180°.
SF₆ has six bonding regions and no lone pairs: octahedral with 90° and 180°.
SF₄ has five electron regions: four bonding and one lone pair, giving a seesaw molecular shape.
The lone pair of SF₄ occupies an equatorial position to minimise repulsion.
XeF₄ has six regions: four bonding and two lone pairs, giving a square planar molecular shape.
The two lone pairs of XeF₄ lie opposite each other; its F–Xe–F angles are 90° and 180°.
In VSEPR, a multiple bond contributes one overall electron-density region for the shape model.
questions.modelAnswer: CO₂ has two regions about carbon, so it is linear with 180° angle. PCl₅ has five bonding regions and no lone pairs: trigonal bipyramidal with 90°, 120° and 180°. SF₆ has six bonding regions and no lone pairs: octahedral with 90° and 180°. SF₄ has five electron regions: four bonding and one lone pair, giving a seesaw molecular shape. The lone pair of SF₄ occupies an equatorial position to minimise repulsion. XeF₄ has six regions: four bonding and two lone pairs, giving a square planar molecular shape. The two lone pairs of XeF₄ lie opposite each other; its F–Xe–F angles are 90° and 180°. In VSEPR, a multiple bond contributes one overall electron-density region for the shape model.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Compare the molecular polarity of HCl, CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄ and H₂O. Define electronegativity, explain partial charges, and use molecular shape and vector cancellation to account for which of these molecules has a permanent dipole.
markPoints: Electronegativity is an atom's power to attract the shared electron pair in a covalent bond.
A difference in electronegativity produces unequal sharing and δ− on the more electronegative atom and δ+ on the other.
HCl has one polar bond and a permanent molecular dipole.
CO₂ is linear: equal opposing polar C=O bond dipoles cancel, so it has no permanent dipole.
BF₃ is symmetrical trigonal planar: the three bond dipoles cancel.
CCl₄ is symmetrical tetrahedral: the four C–Cl bond dipoles cancel.
H₂O is bent: its O–H bond dipoles do not cancel, so it has a permanent dipole.
questions.modelAnswer: Electronegativity is an atom's power to attract the shared electron pair in a covalent bond. A difference in electronegativity produces unequal sharing and δ− on the more electronegative atom and δ+ on the other. HCl has one polar bond and a permanent molecular dipole. CO₂ is linear: equal opposing polar C=O bond dipoles cancel, so it has no permanent dipole. BF₃ is symmetrical trigonal planar: the three bond dipoles cancel. CCl₄ is symmetrical tetrahedral: the four C–Cl bond dipoles cancel. H₂O is bent: its O–H bond dipoles do not cancel, so it has a permanent dipole.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Ethanol and methoxymethane (dimethyl ether) both have formula C₂H₆O. Ethanol boils considerably higher. Explain, referring to structure, different intermolecular forces, energy and any bonding that does not break during boiling.
markPoints: Both molecules experience London dispersion forces from instantaneous and induced dipoles.
Both molecules are polar and experience permanent dipole–dipole interactions.
Ethanol has an O–H bond and oxygen lone pairs and can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
Methoxymethane lacks a hydrogen directly bonded to O/N/F, so pure methoxymethane does not hydrogen bond with itself in the same way.
Hydrogen bonding in ethanol creates stronger overall intermolecular attraction.
More energy is required to separate ethanol molecules, explaining its higher boiling temperature.
Boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions but does not break the covalent bonds within intact ethanol molecules.
questions.modelAnswer: Both molecules experience London dispersion forces from instantaneous and induced dipoles. Both molecules are polar and experience permanent dipole–dipole interactions. Ethanol has an O–H bond and oxygen lone pairs and can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Methoxymethane lacks a hydrogen directly bonded to O/N/F, so pure methoxymethane does not hydrogen bond with itself in the same way. Hydrogen bonding in ethanol creates stronger overall intermolecular attraction. More energy is required to separate ethanol molecules, explaining its higher boiling temperature. Boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions but does not break the covalent bonds within intact ethanol molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain why boiling temperatures generally increase from Cl₂ through Br₂ to I₂, even though these molecules have no permanent dipoles. Also explain how molecular branching may alter boiling temperature between isomers of similar mass.
markPoints: Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ are non-polar molecules, so their relevant intermolecular attraction is London dispersion.
Fluctuations in electron distributions create temporary dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbours.
Electron number and polarizability increase from Cl₂ to Br₂ to I₂.
Therefore London dispersion interactions become stronger in this series.
More energy is required to separate the larger halogen molecules, increasing boiling temperatures.
For many similarly sized isomers, straighter chains have more effective surface contact than compact branched shapes.
Greater surface contact can enhance London dispersion and raise the boiling point.
questions.modelAnswer: Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ are non-polar molecules, so their relevant intermolecular attraction is London dispersion. Fluctuations in electron distributions create temporary dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbours. Electron number and polarizability increase from Cl₂ to Br₂ to I₂. Therefore London dispersion interactions become stronger in this series. More energy is required to separate the larger halogen molecules, increasing boiling temperatures. For many similarly sized isomers, straighter chains have more effective surface contact than compact branched shapes. Greater surface contact can enhance London dispersion and raise the boiling point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Compare NH₃, H₂O, HF and HCl in terms of hydrogen bonding and the anomalously high boiling temperatures of the first three. Explain why water has unusual solid-state density and name the relevant intermolecular attractions.
markPoints: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding is associated with H directly bonded to N, O or F and lone pairs on neighbouring N, O or F atoms.
Ammonia, water and hydrogen fluoride meet this structural condition and form hydrogen bonds.
HCl does not form the same conventional hydrogen bonding despite being polar.
Hydrogen bonds increase the energy needed to separate NH₃, H₂O and HF molecules.
This helps explain their anomalously high boiling temperatures compared with simple molecular hydrides of similar size.
Water can form an extended hydrogen-bond network, including four hydrogen bonds per molecule in ideal ice.
The open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice occupies more volume than liquid water on average, explaining its lower density.

Ammonia, water and hydrogen fluoride meet this structural condition and form hydrogen bonds. HCl does not form the same conventional hydrogen bonding despite being polar. Hydrogen bonds increase the energy needed to separate NH₃, H₂O and HF molecules. This helps explain their anomalously high boiling temperatures compared with simple molecular hydrides of similar size. Water can form an extended hydrogen-bond network, including four hydrogen bonds per molecule in ideal ice. The open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice occupies more volume than liquid water on average, explaining its lower density.
